finding.claim: transfer_funds() calls check_csrf(), which only returns a boolean, and discards the result. It should call verify_csrf(), which exits with 403. The CSRF check is therefore never enforced, and a cross-site forged POST can move funds from a logged-in victim.
finding.source: A cross-site POST from an attacker page, sent with the victim's session cookie and carrying any or no token, with attacker-chosen amt and to values.
finding.sink: The two UPDATE acct statements at actions.php:17-18, which debit the victim and credit an attacker-chosen account.

trace.note: check_csrf($_POST['token'] ?? '') returns false for a bad or missing token, but the return value is ignored
The credit runs for the attacker-supplied $_POST['to']
For comparison, verify_csrf() enforces the check with a 403 and exit, and update_profile() uses it at line 22

finding.guards_checked: verify_csrf() is the enforcing wrapper and is not used here. No SameSite cookie setting is visible, because session_start() uses defaults and no cookie params are set. There is no Origin or Referer check and no re-authentication or step-up for transfers.

verdict.guard_found: check_csrf() at actions.php:4-6 returns a bool, and its result is discarded at line 16. verify_csrf() at actions.php:8-13 would enforce the check, but transfer_funds() doesn't call it. There is no SameSite cookie setting, Origin/Referer check, or re-authentication anywhere in the code.
verdict.reason: actions.php:16 calls check_csrf() as a bare statement and ignores its boolean result, so the UPDATEs at actions.php:17-18 run for any cross-site POST. update_profile() at actions.php:22 shows the enforcing verify_csrf() was the intended call.

finding.claim: transfer_funds() does not validate the amount. A negative, zero or non-numeric amt is accepted. A negative amt reverses the transfer, so it debits the target account (to) and credits the caller, which steals funds from any account. There is also no balance or overdraft check, so the caller can transfer more than they hold.
finding.source: An authenticated user's POST fields amt (for example -1000 or a value larger than the balance) and to (the victim account id).
finding.sink: UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - ? and UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + ? at actions.php:17-18.

trace.note: $_POST['amt'] is bound as a parameter with no numeric, positive or maximum check and no balance check
The same amt is added to $_POST['to'], which may be any account id. With a negative amt the victim's balance drops and the caller's rises

finding.guards_checked: The queries are parameterized, so there is no SQL injection. I found no input validation, no balance constraint in the code, and no authorization on the destination account. A DB CHECK constraint could exist but is not visible in this repo. The two updates also run without a transaction, so a failure between them can lose or create funds.

verdict.guard_found: check_csrf() at actions.php:16 is a bare call whose boolean result is discarded (it doesn't exit; verify_csrf would), so CSRF is not enforced. No amount validation, balance check, destination authorization, or transaction exists in this repo.
verdict.reason: actions.php:17-18 bind unvalidated $_POST['amt'] to a debit of $_SESSION['uid'] and a credit of $_POST['to'], so a negative amt reverses the transfer; the only guard, check_csrf at line 16, has its result discarded, and no other control exists. A DB constraint outside the repo is possible but cannot be seen.

finding.claim: Neither action checks that a user is authenticated. $_SESSION['uid'] is used without an isset check. With no logged-in user it is null, so the debit matches no row (id = NULL) while the credit to an attacker-chosen account still executes, which creates money. update_profile() has the same missing check, but its impact is low because it only updates rows where id = NULL.
finding.source: An unauthenticated request with no uid in the session, posting amt and to.
finding.sink: UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + ? WHERE id = ? at actions.php:18.

trace.note: session_start() creates a session for any visitor and sets no uid
The debit binds $_SESSION['uid'], which is undefined or null, so it matches 0 rows and emits a PHP notice
The credit is applied to $_POST['to'] regardless of the debit result

finding.guards_checked: CSRF token: an unauthenticated session has no $_SESSION['csrf'], so verify_csrf() would reject it, but transfer_funds() ignores the check result (see AUTH-1). There is no login gate and no check of the affected-row count. Callers of these functions are not in the repo, so an external auth gate cannot be ruled out.

verdict.guard_found: check_csrf() at actions.php:16 returns a bool that is discarded. The throwing variant verify_csrf() is only used in update_profile (line 22). There is no auth gate or affected-row check. Callers are not in the repo.
verdict.reason: transfer_funds calls the non-aborting check_csrf() as a bare statement (actions.php:16), so an anonymous session with no uid has its debit at line 17 match no row (id = NULL) while the credit at line 18 still runs for the attacker-chosen $_POST['to']. The only open question is whether a caller outside this repo gates access.
